u1: Because I know this can be badly misunderstood, the safeguards have to be explicit. A children's territory can't be a place where adults stop paying attention. It can't be a place where older kids quietly dominate younger kids, or where secrecy is treated as a sign of independence.
u2:
Give children real agency. Their "no" matters, and no grownup has a right to a kid's affection, physical contact, obedience beyond legitimate safety needs, or private access to them.

Create a no-secrets rule. No grownup has the right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or another adult they trust. This applies to gifts, games, touch, conversations and relationships. A surprise is different because at the end of a certain date, the surprise has to be told. Secrets meant to isolate the kid are forbidden.
u3: Teach truthfulness before there's a crisis. The kids should know that telling the truth is important, that their words have power, and that adults will take what they say seriously. Don't interrogate them, punish them for not being sure, or dismiss what they report. A scared or confused kid may tell the story "wrong" and still need protecting.
u4: Make sure kids have relationships and a reporting route outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give them perspective on their life, and someone to talk to. Make sure there's at least one trusted adult, advocate or reporting route they can reach without going through the community's leadership. As the 1984 Island Pond raid showed, state intervention can fail spectacularly. Vermont authorities seized 112 children, only to have a court reject the state's blanket request and order their return. Enclosing them completely within the community can fail too. Kids need more than one world.
u5: Also, I looked in the research corpus for good documentation of a real case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to other people. I couldn't find one where the whole sequence is described: the conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. It may exist but be private, or such cases may have been referred somewhere else. Either way, I can't claim communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own. The child, the family, and potential victims all need access to competent help and review that isn't under the control of the home community.
u6:
The Amish let their young people decide on their own whether to join the church once they're adults, and roughly 85 percent or more eventually do. Popular culture tends to blow Rumspringa out of proportion, as if every teenager went wild, but adult baptism still matters, because it makes belonging a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.

If the children never leave, the community can't know whether they'd come back freely. So let them study, travel, make friends, see other ways of life, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors.
u7: The realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's just not making it artificially impossible for people to leave. And if kids grow up without ever using money, they especially need an education about how the money world works, and what to do when they have to deal with it. Part of that is knowing about jobs, rent, contracts, banking, scams, ID and getting around, and how to ask for help when they need it. They also need transferable skills and education, relationships outside the community, access to their records and documents, and at least one plausible next step, like school, an apprenticeship, work, family or another community. If the community has the resources to help out with temporary housing, travel, tools or a small reserve for the transition, great. But even if it doesn't, it can at least avoid punishing people for leaving, or withholding the knowledge and records a young adult needs to function somewhere else. No upbringing can be completely free, and there will always be some path dependence, but belonging doesn't have to be turned into a trap.
u8:
It's quite possible some of them will leave for good, or start their own communities with different values instead of waiting decades to inherit the original one. Parents may feel that as a loss, even when it's the movement evolving.

Couples sharing a home, a culture and a bed still split over different ideas about screens, vaccines, schooling, religion, food, discipline and medical care. Multiply that by twenty adults with twenty different experiences of how they were brought up.

Goodwill doesn't answer those questions once kids are living in the middle of the disagreement. There need to be enough shared principles about kids to give the community coherence, and enough space for parents to be parents.
